chapters.title: Chapter 2: A Flicker in the Sun
Chapter 8: The Tree It Won't Show

spans.text: Brick Bloom knelt in the warm light beside the Home exit and re-painted her dot.

It was the smallest job in the whole park, and it was the one she did first, every morning, the way some people start a day with a stretch. A single bright green dot the size of a coin, low on the stone where the arch let you back into Portal Park after a long day in any of the six worlds. She had painted it two weeks ago, the evening after they saved everything. She painted it again now, the same green, the same spot, the same patient brush, and felt the old warm pride settle in her chest like sun on a wall.
We agree this is the route, the dot meant. This door brings you home.
Two weeks it had held. Brick let the green sit a little brighter over the old green and looked at her work, and the thought came easy, the way a thing comes easy when you have stopped questioning it.
Paint it the same and it stays the same.

She had painted it the same green, in the same spot, the same careful way, two weeks running, and the dot had held two weeks. Six worlds, more comings and goings than she could count, and not once had anyone stepped out of the Home arch and gone wait, where am I. She had made a mark, and the mark had stayed, and the staying felt like the most solid thing she had ever built. It was, if she was honest, the proudest thing she had ever made.

She remembered the first night, the one after they saved everything, kneeling in the dark with the gold gone out of the sky and a borrowed lantern and her thumb cold around the brush. She had thought, then, that a mark was a fragile thing, easy to smudge, easy to lose. She had thought she would have to guard it. So every morning since she had come back and laid the green over the green, exactly, the same arc of the brush, the same lean of her hand, because that was how you guarded a thing: you put it back the way it was before the night could take it. Thirteen times now. She could do it with her eyes shut. She liked that she could. It felt like proof.

And under the liking, where she did not look, sat the other shape of it, the one she kept folded small. If the dot held because she painted it the same, then she was the reason it held. She had made a thing that stayed. But if the dot ever scrambled while she was painting it exactly right, then it had never held because of her at all. It had held by luck. And she was not the reason anything stayed. She did not think that thought all the way through. She never did. She just felt its edge sometimes, cold, the way you feel a draft and look for the window and cannot find it, and then went on painting.
It held,
she said, mostly to herself.
Course it held.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip Pop hung upside down off the low wall behind her, antenna brushing the grass.
You painted it. Things you paint stay painted. That is basically your whole thing.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: That is basically my whole thing,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick agreed, and smiled, because it was nice to have a whole thing and have it be true.

The rest of the team sprawled across the grass in the lazy off-duty shapes Brick had learned, over two weeks, to love almost more than the adventures. Six worlds linked, six rules earned, the trouble done, and now just a morning, a gate, and gold pouring down like honey too thick to hurry.
Pip flipped right side up and sized up her audience.
Okay. Why did the portal go to therapy?
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Do not,
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: said Ember Slice, without opening her eyes. She lay flat in the grass with her blue tool-sword balanced across her middle, soaking up sun, doing the most un-Ember thing in the world, which was nothing.
Because,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: said Pip,
it had unresolved exits.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: A warm groaning silence.
That is two jokes about portals having feelings,
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: Ember said.
They are a rich vein. I am not done mining.

Patch Bolt laughed from inside his nest of tools, tightening a bolt on his belt that did not need tightening, because Patch was happiest with something turning under his hands and nothing in the whole park broken.
Keep going. I am easy.
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Off by the reading table, Drip Byte sat with his tablet on his knees, thumbs moving in the small steady way that meant he was logging something. Brick watched him a beat. Drip had been quiet all morning, but Drip was often quiet, and the cyan glow on his face looked content enough.
What is the verdict,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick called over.
Are we good?
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: We are good.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip tapped his screen.
Translating block six. Logging it now.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Real pride sat under the words.
Sixth one. It is holding still long enough to read. Two weeks ago it would not sit for a scan.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Read it out,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: said Pip.
I like when the broken ones start to make words.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Drip turned the tablet. A small symbol glowed there, neat and cyan, a block that had stopped flickering, its green crack frozen and tamed into something the screen could finally hold.
Not a whole word yet,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: he said.
A piece of one. But it is ours now. It is in the ledger. It cannot get lost.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Six down,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: said Patch.
Six readable,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip corrected, gentle.
The rest still flicker. But six is six.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Brick stood, knees stiff, and looked up at the Master Gate, and let herself feel it all at once.

The gate rose over the whole park, taller than the orchard trees, its stone face warm in the climbing light. Six world-badges ringed it, each lit from inside: a green hill, a red canyon, a blue cave, a pale sky, a silver gear, and a violet swirl for the park itself. Six small suns in a circle, all awake, all earned.

And in the dead center of the ring, where a seventh badge should sit, there was the pale slot. Empty. Smooth. Waiting. It did not glow. It never had. Brick looked at it the way you look at a chair at the table that has always been there and always been empty: you stop expecting it to fill, but you never quite stop noticing it.

Then her eyes dropped to the lower part of the gate, where the trouble lived, and where it had stopped living. Twelve small black cubes still flickered along the bottom of the frame. That was the count. Brick knew it without counting, the way you know how many steps are in your own stairs. There had been more at the worst of it, drifting and mislabeling and forgetting. The team had pinned two of them down in the saving of the park, read them, tamed them, turned them from nonsense into something the ledger could keep. But the gate-count was the count Brick trusted, the one she could see. Twelve. Twelve little black blocks, still going on, off, on, their green cracks spelling half-shapes that came apart before you could read them.

They did not drift anymore. The team had given them a place to flicker, a low ledge along the gate, in the open, where Drip could watch them and the worst of their misrouting could not reach the routes. Twelve glitches, parked. Twelve broken things, waiting their turn to be read, none of them destroyed, because you did not destroy a thing that was only trying to say something. You read it.

Brick looked from the twelve flickering blocks to her own bright green dot, low on the Home arch, holding steady. The blocks flickered because nobody had pinned their shape down yet. The dot held because she kept its shape exactly. Simple. Steady. The same brush, the same place, and the route stayed true. That was the whole secret of a mark, far as Brick could see. You held the shape, the shape held the meaning, and the meaning held the path.
Behind her, Pip had gone quiet.
Not asleep-quiet. The other kind. The kind where her antenna stilled and the little heart on her chest pulsed once, soft, and she turned a thing over before she said it.
Or,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: said Pip.
Brick looked back at her.
Or it stays,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: said Pip,
because we still mean it.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Brick did not know what to do with that, at first.
It is the same paint,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: she said.
Sure.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip was not arguing. Pip never quite argued; she just set a different shape down next to yours and let you look at both.
But you did not paint it for the paint. You painted it so that when somebody comes home tired and a little turned around, they see the green and they know: home, this way, you made it.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: She tipped her head.
That is not the green. That is us, still meaning it. You could paint it a hundred more times, and if one day nobody meant it anymore, it would just be a dot.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Brick looked at her dot. It looked, to her, exactly like a dot that meant home. She could not see the difference Pip was pointing at. Paint it the same and it stays the same, and it stays because we still mean it, to Brick, standing in the gold with green on her thumb, felt like the same sentence said two ways. The dot was the same. The meaning was the same. Why would you separate them?
I think those are the same thing,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: she said.
Maybe.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip smiled and let it go, because that was a Pip thing too, say the true thing once, plainly, and then do not push it.
You would know. It is your whole thing.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: It is my whole thing,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick agreed, and the easiness came back, and she believed it all the way.
She filed Pip's words in the place she kept things she was not ready to think about. The folder, lately, was not as empty as she liked.
Captain Cubemelon was the only one not lying down.

He stood near the gate with the Gravity Wrench resting easy across his shoulder, his blue lens half-lidded against the brightness, watching the morning the way he watched everything, like he was counting it and finding the count good. But he was not counting steps out loud, and he was not measuring anything, and most of all he was not looking at the arch.

The locked arch stood off to the left of the Master Gate, the way a closed door stands at the edge of a sunny kitchen. Tall stone curve, filled with dark, a clean little half-cube-and-a-line cut into its keystone. It hummed, faintly, always. For a long time the Captain had not been able to keep his lens off it. Now he stood with his face to the orchard and his back half to the arch, and let it hum, and did not reach for it.
Brick noticed, the way you notice good weather. She did not say anything. You did not make a thing of it, with the Captain. You just let him not-rush the arch, and were glad.
We could open a world,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Patch said hopefully from his tool-nest.
Just to stretch our legs. Green Hills, maybe. The orchards are nice this time of year.
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: No rush,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: said the Captain.
I am not rushing. I am suggesting.
Suggestion noted.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: The Captain's mouth did the small thing that, on him, counted as a grin.
We earned a slow morning. Slow.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: He said the word the way he said it to himself first, Slow, and then to the team, soft, a rule he was keeping on purpose.
The routes are stable. The dot held two weeks. Let it be a slow morning.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: He is not wrong,
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: said Moss.

Two words, from the big green shape standing quiet at the edge of it all, shield resting against his shoulder. Brick looked over. Moss was not watching the orchard or the jokes. Moss was watching the Captain not-rush the arch, the way Moss watched all the things that might pull at the people he stood between. And what Moss saw seemed to ease him by one degree, because his shoulders came down a notch, and he let the shield settle.
He is not wrong,
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: Moss said again, which from Moss was practically a speech.
Brick grinned and bent to clean her brush. Seven of them. The whole circle, off duty in the gold, and the dot held, and nothing in the world needed fixing.
And then, far out at the thin edge of the park, where the gold ran out into the morning blue, something flickered.
Brick almost missed it. Everyone almost missed it. It was so small, and so far, and so deeply not where a flicker was supposed to be.

The twelve blocks flickered down on the gate's ledge. That was allowed. That was where they lived. But this one sat out past the last of the trees, out where the routes ran toward Green Hills, alone, in the open. A small black square going on, off, on, a green crack reaching. And then it caught the sun.
It caught the sun.

That was the wrong part. Brick felt it a half-second before her head explained it, the way you feel a wrong note in a song before you can name which one. The glitches hid in shadow. They hated the high light; everyone knew that, in the loose way you know things about your home. They flickered at the edge of evening, in seams, in the dark. They did not sit out in a square of full gold and flicker anyway, small and stubborn and tired, like something that had run out of dark to hide in and decided to be seen.

It flickered once more, in the sun, where it never should have been. And Brick, watching it, did not feel afraid. That surprised her, after. She felt the way you feel when you find a small bird sitting on the open path in full daylight, too tired to fly, and your first thought is not that it is dangerous but that something has gone wrong for it, that it would be in the hedge if it could, that it is out here because it has run out of better places to be.

There was a small sound, half a green flicker, FZZZT, a worn and tired sound, not a hungry one. It was the sound a thing makes when it is very tired of hiding. Then it went dark, resting, the way frightened things go quiet when they have worn themselves out, and the spot where it had been was just empty gold, and Brick could not have sworn, after, that she had seen anything at all.
Did you,
she started.
Yeah.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip was already on her feet, antenna up, little heart pulsing fast. She was not laughing now.
Brick. That was in the sun.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: The Captain had turned. His lens was wide open now, a thin blue scan-line spilling out toward the edge of the park, careful, not rushed. He did not reach for the arch. He looked at the orchard line.
Drip. Tell me the routes are green.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: A pause. The scrape of Drip's thumbs on glass. Then, in a voice Brick did not like at all, a voice gone careful, the way Drip went careful when the screen said one thing and the room said another:
They are green,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip said.
The screen says they are green.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: That is not a yes,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: said the Captain.
No,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip admitted.
It is not.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Brick looked down at her dot, low on the Home arch, bright and steady and two weeks held. Paint it the same and it stays the same. It looked exactly as true as it had a minute ago. That was the part that nagged at her, though she could not have said why. The dot looked exactly as true. But a thing could look exactly as true as it had a minute ago and not be, the way the routes were green on the screen and not, somehow, a yes. She turned that over and did not like the shape of it, and set it down quick, the way you set down a hot pan.
What does the screen say is wrong,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Patch asked, half up out of his tool-nest now, a wrench already in his hand though he was not reaching for anything with it, just holding it the way some people hold a railing.
That is the trouble,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip said.
It does not say anything is wrong. It says everything is fine. That is what I do not like.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: He looked up from the glass, and the cyan glow on his face had gone thin.
A thing that is broken tells you it is broken. This is telling me it is fine, and the room is telling me it is not, and I trust the room.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Slow,
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: said Moss, from the edge, watching all of them at once.
Slow,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain agreed, and did not reach for the arch, and did not rush.
We look first. We do not fix what we have not read.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Out past the orchard line, in the empty gold where the flicker had been, the morning went very, very quiet. Quiet the way a map goes quiet when it has begun, somewhere out at its edge, to forget a route it was sure of.
Get your sketchpad,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain said.
We are going to go look at it.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Brick was already reaching for it. But her eyes were on her dot, and for the first time in two weeks, she found herself wondering, only a little, only for a heartbeat, whether painting it the same was really the same as keeping it true.
She stood and tucked the brush away and did not say the wondering out loud. It went into the folder with Pip's words, the not-empty folder, and the lid did not quite close on it this time.

Seven of them gathered toward the orchard line. The dot held behind them, bright and green and sure. Out at the edge of the park, a frightened thing rested in a square of light it had no business sitting in, and somewhere past it, gentle as a name going thin on the tongue, the morning had already begun to forget the way through.
